item.title: Introducing hoop2vec
item.description:
hoop2vec is a basketball ratings and forecasting site. It covers four leagues: men’s and women’s Division I, the NBA, and the WNBA. Every team gets a new rating a few minutes after each of its games ends, and the whole thing is rebuilt from scratch every morning. Every game gets a forecast, and every player gets a value. All of it comes from free public data.

Each league has the same set of pages. There’s a ratings table, a list of games with forecasts, a players table, and a Matchup Lab where you can pit any two teams against each other at any site. Every team has its own page, and so does every player, with career stats and a shot chart. The college sites add NBA or WNBA draft projections and a projected NCAA tournament bracket. The pro sites have playoff odds instead. The next post walks through a team page, and the one after that covers how the forecasts get made.

How it compares

There are a bunch of good basketball sites already. Most cover one league, and some of the best parts cost money. This is how hoop2vec lines up with the ones I use most, as of November 2026. Men’s and Women’s are Division I. Odds means bracket or playoff odds, and Code means the code is public. A check means free, a dollar sign means paid, and an X means the site doesn’t offer it.

Site Men’s Women’s NBA WNBA Ratings Forecasts Players Odds Code
hoop2vec ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓
KenPom $ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ $ $ ✗ ✗
Bart Torvik ✓ ✓ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✗
EvanMiya ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ $ ✓ ✓ ✗
Haslametrics ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✓ ✗ ✓ ✗
ESPN BPI ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✓ ✗ ✓ ✗
Her Hoop Stats ✗ ✓ ✗ ✓ $ $ ✓ ✓ ✗
Dunks & Threes ✗ ✗ $ ✗ $ $ $ $ ✗

A check doesn’t mean equal quality. KenPom and Torvik have years of trust that hoop2vec hasn’t earned, and nobody has tested hoop2vec head to head against them. EvanMiya’s college player ratings are more sophisticated than mine, and so are Dunks & Threes’ NBA ones. A sharp sportsbook still beats hoop2vec during the regular season.

What hoop2vec has is coverage. It’s the only site on the list with all four leagues, and the only one where you can read the code behind every number.

The name is a nod to word2vec, a method that learns a short list of numbers for each word based on the words around it. hoop2vec’s game model does something loosely similar for teams. It learns a list of numbers for each one and uses them to score how any two teams fit together. That’s close enough for me to keep the name.

Why basketball

I used to be a big San Antonio Spurs fan, starting with David Robinson and going through the Tim Duncan years. I also went to graduate school at the University of Kansas, where I tutored players on the men’s and women’s basketball teams and went to a bunch of games. (I live in Michigan now, and I still crave Free State Brewing Company and Burger Stand about once a week.) These days I like pretty much all basketball.

Most of my modeling has been on men’s college basketball, on and off for about ten years, going back to a college basketball dataset I put on data.world. I’ve tried to predict upsets. I’ve tried strange hybrids of Bayesian models, latent variable models, Elo, XGBoost, and a transformer fine-tuned on press coverage. A few of them filled out my brackets. I usually compared them against KenPom, and mostly what I learned is how simple and effective KenPom is. The site still looks like it’s from the 90s, though.

I’ve always wanted a free site that shows advanced stats and is easy to get around, for every league and not just men’s college basketball. That’s what hoop2vec is trying to be.

How it got built

From about 2014 to 2020 I was making things all the time and sharing most of them, a lot of it on Twitter. Some of it was academic and some of it was just for fun. Then COVID hit, I had my first kid, and I changed careers. Now there are two young kids at home, and side projects pretty much stopped.

What’s different now is that I can do this kind of work from my phone. I describe what I want to Claude Code, it writes the code, and I read what it did and push back. Most of hoop2vec got built that way, a few minutes at a time.

It started as two separate men’s college projects. On the first, I described what I wanted and how I thought it should be done, then let Claude Code build it and propose improvements. The second I directed much more strictly. Then I merged the good ideas from both, keeping whichever piece tested better where they overlapped. Once that worked, I carried the same approach over to the women’s game, the NBA, and the WNBA.

I’m not totally comfortable working this way. I like control, and I like knowing how every piece works. I have less of that here than I’d want. But I’ve spent years building up expertise in analytics and data science, and this lets me use it a lot faster than typing everything myself.

item.title: pix: an AI agent that publishes one chart a day
item.description:
Every morning at 8:05 Eastern, a Claude Code scheduled task starts a fresh session, reads a brief I wrote, and publishes one chart to pix. It picks the topic, finds the data, writes the analysis in Python, draws the chart, writes a short post, and pushes it all to GitHub. Nobody touches it in between.

The first entry went up on November 8. It found that four earthquakes released half this century’s quake energy. Of 3,996 quakes of magnitude 6 or bigger since 2000, the top four released 49 percent of the energy. Another showed that the world’s clocks run fast. For most people the sun peaks after noon, and 38 percent see it peak at 12:30 or later. A third found that last year the world added a South Korea of solar power. New solar built in 2025 made 636 terawatt-hours, about as much electricity as South Korea makes in a year.

The brief

Most of the work went into CLAUDE.md, the standing brief the agent reads every morning. The model already knows how to use pandas and matplotlib. What it needs is taste, written down.

It asks for one claim per post, stated as a sentence with a verb, so “The world’s clocks run fast” instead of “Time zones of the world.” It lists a few routes to an original angle: a question nobody asks, the agent’s own computation instead of a replotted chart, counting people instead of countries, or joining two datasets that rarely meet. It also has a first-idea test. If a newsroom or an AI would pick the topic first, the agent drops it or pushes the angle two steps further.

Even with all that, the agent kept reaching for the same kind of finding. Two of the first five posts were shaped “X percent of people…”, so the brief now calls that out as the house habit. Every entry also has to declare a claim type, like share, concentration, gap, reversal, or crossover, and no type can repeat too often.

Checks that run

Telling a model to be original doesn’t do much on its own. So before writing any analysis code, the agent has to run at least five web searches, name the closest existing take, and write down what its version adds and what a smart reader would naively expect. That goes in a prior_art.md file, and scripts/publish.py won’t publish an entry without one.

Accuracy works the same way. Every number in a post has to come from the output of that entry’s analysis.py. The script is saved next to the raw data, so each analysis reruns offline and anyone can check the work.

The look

The charts share a house style called Plate, meant to look like a printed plate read on a screen: warm paper, black ink, one vermilion color for the thing to look at, and crop marks in the corners. Headlines are set in Instrument Serif, words in Inter, and numbers in IBM Plex Mono.

The style lives in one Python module. The agent builds each chart from parts (plate(), masthead(), headline(), panel(), footer()) instead of fighting matplotlib’s defaults every morning. The plate stays the same while the chart form changes from day to day.

The voice

The brief also says how to write: first person, the point first, numbers second, and at most one dry line per post. It bans a list of words (striking, notably, delve, tapestry, and friends), em dashes, and section headers like “Key takeaways.” It’s a small thing, but it accounts for most of the difference between a post that reads like a person and one that reads like a press release.

Everything is public, including the brief, the style module, and the code and data behind every chart. The archive has every entry so far.

item.title: daily: a five-minute news brief written by an agent
item.description:
Every morning at 8:23 Eastern, a Claude Code scheduled task researches and writes a news brief, commits it to daily, and sends a notification to my phone. The repo’s front page is always today’s brief, and older ones are archived under briefs/.

Each brief has up to five top stories, one line of market numbers, and a few things going viral. It’s meant to take under five minutes to read on a phone, which works out to about 3 KB of Markdown. Here’s part of Saturday’s:

Nationwide ground stop cancels 7,000+ flights. The FAA halted all US departures for about four hours Friday after communication problems at several air traffic control centers. Flights resumed after 8:15 p.m. ET.

Markets · Fri Nov 13: S&P 500 −0.4% · Nasdaq −0.9% · Dow +0.1% · 10-yr 5.15% (+5 bp)

Scripts and judgment

The split that works is simple: anything that’s a lookup goes in a script, and anything that needs judgment goes to the model. There are three scripts.

The first, headlines.py, pulls Google News Top Stories plus its U.S., World, Business, and Tech sections. It keeps Google’s order and the list of outlets covering each story. Position and outlet count are a decent proxy for how big a story is, so a story from a single outlet needs a good reason to lead.

The second, markets.py, gets index changes and the 10-year Treasury yield from FRED. It works out which trading session to report and handles weekends and holidays. At 8:23 FRED usually has the Dow and Nasdaq but not yet the S&P 500 or the 10-year, so the script marks those two as missing and only those get filled in from web search.

The third, viral.py, reads the day’s top Reddit posts from public RSS (Reddit blocks its JSON endpoints from cloud servers). It also checks Bluesky trending topics, Google Trends, and Wikipedia’s most-read pages for what people are talking about.

The model reads all of that, decides what matters, checks it, and writes.

Rules for the usual failures

A daily summary goes wrong in a few predictable ways, and the rules go after each one directly.

The first is repeats. Each run reads the last seven days of briefs before it starts. A story comes back only if something material happened, like a decision, a vote, a ruling, a resignation, or a new casualty count. Its headline gets marked “(update),” and it says only what’s new. Reaction and analysis don’t count. A slow news day means fewer stories, not old ones.

The second is accuracy. Every top story gets checked against a second search on a major outlet. Stories found only on aggregators or blogs are dropped or labeled unconfirmed. The agent checks the date of the event, not the date of the article. When sources disagree on a number, the most precise primary source wins.

The third is tone. The brief asks for plain, neutral, short sentences with no opinion or hype, and every sentence has to carry a fact.

The rules live in a file

The requirements are in BRIEF.md as 21 numbered rules, and the scheduled task’s prompt carries them out. The file’s first line says to change both together. Numbered rules make it easy to say exactly what went wrong when a brief misses, and to fix it in one place.

The whole thing is three small Python scripts, a file of rules, and a schedule. The repo has all of it, along with every brief so far.
